facts.fact: Shoaling means fish staying together in a group for social reasons. Each fish swims fairly independently but stays near the others.
A shoal becomes a school when its members swim at the same speed and in the same direction. Schooling fish are usually one species and of similar age and size.
Shoaling fish keep to loose groups in one area and may be of different species. Schooling fish move together in the same direction, at the same speed and at the same time.
Living in a group helps fish spot predators and lowers each fish's chance of being caught. It also helps them find food and mates.
About one quarter of fish species shoal all their lives, and about half shoal for part of their lives.
Group size can change a fish's aggression, darting, shoaling behaviour and neophobia (fear of new things).
Groups of aquarium fish in the wild range from two or three to more than twenty fish.
Group species commonly sold for aquariums include tetras, barbs, danios, rasboras, rainbowfish, some loaches and Corydoras catfish.

In a University of Plymouth study, neon tetras (Paracheirodon innesi) and white cloud mountain minnows (Tanichthys albonubes) were kept alone, in pairs, in groups of five, or in groups of 10, in 10-liter tanks for two weeks.
In that study, lone fish fought more and behaved less like wild fish. Fish in groups of 10 were the least aggressive, darted least and shoaled most.
Neon tetras (Paracheirodon innesi) and white cloud mountain minnows (Tanichthys albonubes) dart less and are less aggressive in larger groups. The page links darting to fear and stress.
A White Cloud Mountain minnow (Tanichthys albonubes) kept alone may become timid and lose its bright colour.
Schooling fish kept in larger groups are less stressed, more colourful and less skittish.
Cá bơi theo đàn kept in small groups become stressed and timid and lose colour. Cá Neon hide in the plants when there are only a few of them.
Tiger barbs (Puntigrus tetrazona) nip and chase each other to set up a hierarchy, which is normal inside their own group.
Buy schooling fish in groups of at least 6, and more if the tank is large enough.
The researchers advised keeping neon tetras (Paracheirodon innesi) and white cloud mountain minnows (Tanichthys albonubes) in home aquariums in groups of at least 10.
Neon tetras (Paracheirodon innesi) must be kept in groups of at least six. They are more active in groups of about eight to 12 or more.
White Cloud Mountain minnows (Tanichthys albonubes) feel most comfortable in a group of at least five.
Tiger barbs (Puntigrus tetrazona) do best in schools of at least eight to a dozen fish, and more is better.
Cá bơi theo đàn need at least 5–6 fish, and 8–15 is ideal for a clear schooling effect.
Choose a long, wide tank with plenty of swimming room over a tall, narrow one.
Small schooling species need a tank about 40–60 cm long, and a longer tank helps the group hold formation. Larger schooling fish need a tank of 90 cm to 1.5 m.
The tank should be fully cycled before Cá Sóc Đầu Đỏ are added.
Keep fish in groups only if the species evolved to live in groups, because the effects of grouping differ between species.
A common beginner mistake is buying one or two fish each of many different schooling species.
Keeping only 2–3 cá bơi theo đàn is a common mistake, because no group forms.
A tank that is too small or overcrowded leaves no room for the fish to swim as a group.
Keeping schooling fish with aggressive or large fish gets them chased and splits the school.
A strong current or light that is too bright breaks the school apart. Gentle to moderate filter flow is advised.
Tiger barbs (Puntigrus tetrazona) harass slow, long-finned fish such as angelfish and guppies and chew up their fins, so do not keep them together.
Do not mix short-finned and long-finned tiger barbs (Puntigrus tetrazona), because the long-finned ones are at a disadvantage.
Keeping more than one male Siamese fighting fish in a tank harms their welfare, so not every species should be kept in groups.
Cá Trâm spend most of their time fleeing when kept with large or aggressive fish.
Cá Neon are small and can be bullied, so the page advises against keeping them with aggressive fish such as Ali and Thần tiên. Plants and rocks give them shelter.
The neon tetra's scientific name is Paracheirodon innesi.
The White Cloud Mountain minnow's scientific name is Tanichthys albonubes.
Keeping more fish together can work better against fighting than separating the fighters, according to Tony Farrell of the University of British Columbia.
Name for the term: "cá bơi thành đàn"
Name for the term: "cá cảnh bơi theo đàn"

A Vietnamese shop advises keeping cá bơi thành đàn in groups of 3 pairs or more to avoid stress.
Cá Trâm (Boraras urophthalmoides) live in large shoals and form a block of colour. A Vietnamese shop sells them at 40–50 thousand đồng per 100 fish.
Cá tam giác (Trigonostigma heteromorpha) is gentle and easy to keep. A Vietnamese shop sells it at 6,000–8,000 đồng per fish.
Cá sóc đầu đỏ (Hemigrammus rhodostomus) is also called cá mũi đỏ or hồng thủ, and looks best when many are kept together.
Diếc Anh Đào (Puntius titteya), also called cá Anh Đào, is gentle and can share a tank with other fish.
Cá Xecan, also called cá Tứ vân, is aggressive and nips fins. It should not be kept with long-finned fish such as ba đuôi and thần tiên.
Cá NEON sold in Vietnam include Neon Xanh, Neon Vua, Neon Hoàng Đế and Neon Đen. The shop says they are not easy to keep and need skill.
Cá Tam giác (Harlequin Rasbora) should be stocked at least 10 at a time. Suggested conditions are 23-28°C, pH 5.5-7.5 and a tank of about 40 L.
Cá Neon (Neon Tetra): suggested conditions are 20-26°C, hardness 5-20 dH, pH 5-7 and a tank of about 70 L.
Cá Sóc đầu đỏ (Rummy Nose Tetra): suggested conditions are 22-26°C, hardness 5-11 dH, pH 5.5-7 and a tank of about 80 L.
Cá Chim cánh cụt (Hockey Stick Tetra) is listed as a schooling fish for planted tanks: 22-28°C, pH 5.5-8.0, a tank of about 80 L.
Cá Neon need 15 or more fish to stay confident and show good colour.
Cá Sóc Đầu Đỏ: minimum tank 60 L, 24–28°C, pH 6.0–7.0, swims in the middle and bottom of the tank.
"Neon Vua" is used as the Vietnamese name for Cardinal Tetra.
